Title: The Nineties: A Blast from Britain's Musical, Fashion and Sporting Past Subtitle: Britpop, Spice Mania and Football's Homecoming In the heart of the 1990s, a resurgence of British culture rode over the horizon like a storm. Britannia, the goddess, was awoken – and she came back with a vengeance. The decade gave birth to Britpop, a musical revolution that touted "Cool Britannia" and socialism. The Spice Girls took over the charts, and suddenly, gender and fashion were very political. Meanwhile, football returned to its roots as England hosted the 1996 European Championship finals. At the center of the Britpop phenomenon were bands like Oasis, Blur, and Pulp. They weren't just making music; they were painting the sound of a generation, capturing the raw emotion of the early '90s Britain – the "Cool Britannia" that Prime Minister Tony Blair and his government celebrated. Music, fashion, and politics blended together in a way that was quintessentially British. The clothes were eclectic, reflecting the influence of various subcultures. Fashion was never uni-directional, with grunge, punk, or even preppy styles weaving in and out of this mosaic. One moment you'd see a girl in a Union Jack dress; the next, she'd be sporting heavy eyeliner, scrawling anarchy symbols on her backpack. Styling was about expressing identity – to the core, the essence of the individual. Yet, 1996 delivered a more unifying experience: football came home, as summarised in one of the most catchy slogans for the European Championship finals. England, the spiritual home of the beautiful game, hosted the tournament. The atmosphere leading up to and during the event was electric. The country was gripped in anticipation, with the iconic 'Three Lions' anthem blasting on all radio stations and TVs. English football was at the heart of the British cultural festivities, embodying national pride, spirit, and a collective belonging. The Britpop bands didn’t miss this unique opportunity to tap into the football's emotional resonance. Songs like "World in Motion" by New Order and the England football squad, or even Blur’s "Parklife," lent their tunes to a spirit that rolled from music halls to soccer stadiums. The Spice Girls, in turn, represented another take on the nation’s cultural identity, one that was unapologetically Brit, playful, and leading in the charge for women’s empowerment. The Nineties cultural boom wasn't just about entertainment or sporting triumphs; it was about national self-confidence and reinvention. It was a decade where Britain looked inward and outwards simultaneously, finding something new to shout about while still holding onto the sumptuous heritage that was often too close for comfort. The unique clashing and melding of the old and new, left and right, in the spirit of Britpop, the Spice Girls, and the homecoming of football, created a period that felt as much about the future as it did about reviving the past, proudly and cheekily so. It wasn't all rainbows and unicorns, however. The late '90s also saw debates and protests against the government's austerity measures and a rise in issues like xenophobia and nationalism. Their extensive study, published in Cell, delves into the ways in which the virus adapted – suggesting far-reaching implications for future outbreaks and the development of potential therapies. The research team focused on analyzing the genetic sequences of the Ebola virus samples collected from patients at the early stages of the epidemic, primarily in Guinea and Sierra Leone. They found that the virus underwent "major and rapid genetic changes" in these early months, particularly among a segment of its genome known as the glycoprotein – the part responsible for infecting cells. These changes, or mutations, significantly improved the virus's ability to bind to and enter human cells. Uncovering this genetic shift in the virus's evolutionary path gives us a deeper understanding of the rapid spread of the 2014-15 outbreak, the deadliest in history. Ebola, also known as EVD (Ebola Virus Disease), was discovered in 1976 in what was then Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Before 2014, the disease had never caused such a massive scale outbreak, claiming tens of thousands of lives across West Africa. Dr. Jeremy Luban, the study's co-author from the University of Massachusetts Medical School, explained the importance of understanding these adaptations: "If we can learn more about how Ebola evolved to become so infectious in humans so quickly, we might be able to prevent, or at least mitigate, future outbreaks in several ways." One key area of exploration is the potential development of therapeutic interventions. "Perhaps some of these genetic changes that improved the virus's ability to infect human cells could also become drug targets," Luban suggested. The research could provide a roadmap for scientists to focus on when developing drugs or vaccines. The adaptations that helped the 2014-15 Ebola strain infect human tissues with such ease may also explain the high mortality rate associated with that outbreak. The study suggests that while the Ebola virus generally doesn't mutate as rapidly as some other viruses, when changing the key parts of its genome related to cell infection, these changes can be quite significant. Dr. Pardis Sabeti, another co-author of the study and a computational biologist at the Broad Institute, emphasized the need for rapid public health responses to future outbreaks. "Understanding how Ebola was evolving in real time during the 2014-15 outbreak allows us to better prepare for future responses. Clearly, these adaptations occurred rapidly, within months, not years. This gives us a window into how Ebola reacts to our interventions – something that will be crucial if we hope to contain outbreaks more effectively in the future." This new understanding of Ebola's rapid adaptation also challenges any notion that the disease can always be contained by traditional public health measures alone. It highlights the necessity for improved diagnostic tools, potential prophylactic treatments (to be used in high-risk groups), and vaccines. The findings come at a time when the global health community is already grappling with the complexities of future epidemics. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has cast a light on the urgent need for rapid detection, intervention, and research into fast-mutating viruses. Libya: Five Years into Unrest, Still without a United Government Five years have passed since the unrest that would eventually lead to the overthrow and killing of Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi began. During these five years, despite numerous efforts and international interventions, Libya remains without a single government with authority over the whole country. The ousting and killing of Gaddafi may have marked a new chapter in Libyan history, but the chaos that followed has left deep scars and division across the nation, suggesting that the Libyan people's journey towards stability and peace is far from over. Evidence of this can be seen in the current political scenario in Libya. Since 2011, the country has been divided between two main factions, with each having its own internationally recognized government. The government based in Tobruk, supported by a military force led by General Khalifa Haftar, has a presence in the east of the country. Meanwhile, the government based in Tripoli, which has been internationally recognized, claims control over the western part of Libya. This division not only splits the government but also the military, economy, and society at large. The resulting power vacuum has served as fertile ground for the rise of various militias and extremist groups. Groups like the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) have exploited this lack of authority to gain a foothold, causing further instability and suffering for the Libyan people. Their influence has been felt most notably in areas such as Derna and parts of Sirte, where they have waged a violent campaign, including horrific acts like the beheading of local residents and foreigners alike. Internationally, the response to the ongoing crisis in Libya has been mixed and often ineffective. While the United Nations, European Union, and other global powers have taken efforts to facilitate negotiations and socio-political reforms, these interventions have achieved limited success in uniting the two opposing governments and bringing an end to the conflict. One of the primary challenges has been the different interests and priorities of the various international players involved in resolving the Libyan crisis. While the international community broadly agrees on the need for stability in Libya, there are differing views on how best to achieve this. Some countries, like Egypt and the UAE, support the Tobruk-based government and General Haftar, viewing them as a bulwark against extremism. Others, more aligned with the Tripoli-based government, see Haftar as a force exacerbating divisions. The US, while involved, has maintained a somewhat passive stance, focusing more on counter-terrorism efforts rather than leading a unified diplomatic push. Furthermore, internal divisions within the various factions of the Libyan political and social spectrum have complicated the prospects for peace and unity. The country's inherently tribal nature, combined with the differing ideologies of those vying for power, has made it difficult to forge a broad consensus behind any particular political entity or leader. The economic consequences of this ongoing unrest should also not be underestimated. Oil production, Libya's primary source of revenue, has been significantly impacted by the conflict. Due to the presence of different militaries and militias controlling different parts of oil producing regions, there have been frequent disruptions to production and export, crippling an already fragile economy. The Libyan people, already suffering from political uncertainty and violence, have to deal with a worsening economic crisis, with shortages of essential goods, a plummeting Libyan dinar, and increasing unemployment. Education and healthcare services, once considered to be among the most developed in Africa under Gaddafi's rule, have also suffered. With the pressures of a constantly evolving curriculum, budget cuts and increases in pupil numbers, the job keeps getting tougher for those at the frontline. Public sector unions, such as the National Education Union (NEU) and the NASUWT, have been vocal about this issue for months. They have cited a variety of reasons for the staff shortfall, including low pay, excessive workload, and concerns over job security - factors making the profession less attractive to new recruits and leading to high turnover rates among existing staff. "It's not just theoretical. We are talking about classrooms with no qualified teacher in front of them for weeks or sometimes even months. The workforce gaps in education are a symptom of a broader systemic issue that requires a multifaceted approach. These images are then being used to identify and address the perpetrators, with the intention of recovering the stolen fuel costs and preventing similar incidents in the future. But it's not just the filmmakers and activists speaking out against this new Act. The monitoring of individuals at service stations raises questions about state surveillance and data protection. The ICO stated that it has been in touch with the PSNI and is "considering the matter." Campaigners, meanwhile, are arguing that these changes, alongside the recently implemented rules for pornography, represent a slippery slope towards stricter regulations on personal freedoms and expression. They are calling for parliamentary and public scrutiny to ensure that such measures are not used to erode civil liberties and personal autonomy. The face-sitting protests – a unique and unconventional form of protest that evidently intends to shock and raise awareness – reflect the intensity of feelings among those opposed to the new pornography bans. Equally, the PSNI's fuel theft scheme, while distinct from the pornography debate, has sparked similar concerns about the regulation of personal activities and the balance between law enforcement and civil freedom. Undoubtedly, these are sensitive and complex issues. On one hand, preventing crime and ensuring public safety are critical responsibilities of government and law enforcement agencies. On the other, there is a need to protect fundamental rights and freedoms and to ensure that the means used to achieve these goals are just, proportionate, and respectful of individual privacy. The vaccine, which targets rotavirus, a highly contagious virus that can cause severe vomiting and diarrhea in young children, drastically increases their risk of dehydration and other complications – in some cases putting them at risk of death. As a result of these promising trials, the companies behind the vaccine, GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) and Seattle-based biotech company SK Bioscience, are now preparing for larger-scale efficacy trials that will be critical in determining its potential widespread use. This early success has sparked widespread optimism among health professionals, with Dr. Sandeep Jain, a pediatrician with the World Health Organization, stating that "a safe and effective rotavirus vaccine is long overdue." The trial results, which have just been published in the prestigious journal 'The Lancet', indicate that the new vaccine appears to have produced a strong immune response in adults, a key marker of potential effectiveness. Rotavirus accounts for a staggering 20% of childhood deaths worldwide, with the majority of these deaths occurring in countries where healthcare infrastructure is less sophisticated. In developed countries like the UK, it's estimated that approximately 1 in 4 infants and young children will suffer from a rotavirus infection before they turn 5, causing severe bouts of illness that often require hospital treatment. The need for an improved vaccine is evident. While two existing vaccines – Rotarix and RotaTeq – have been successfully used globally to reduce rotavirus infections, studies have shown that they are less effective in preventing severe cases in developing countries where they are most desperately needed. They also have shown to be less effective in preventing all types of rotavirus and may not provide long-term protection. This doesn't come a moment too soon. Last year's global progress report from the World Health Organization and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) highlighted that "rotavirus continues to be a leading cause of diarrhea-related deaths in young children." What makes this new vaccine particularly exciting is not only its potential to protect against a wider range of rotavirus strains, but also the possibility that it could be more effective in areas where vaccines are currently underperforming. The Phase I trial was carried out on 150 healthy adult participants – a typical first step for any new vaccine to assess safety and stimulate an immune response. The volunteers were divided into three groups, given different doses of the vaccine or a placebo. The results were promising: the new vaccine was well-tolerated, and all vaccine recipients produced antibodies against the rotavirus in quantities that meet or exceed what is considered protective levels. The next phase of trials will involve hundreds of children across several continents. If successful, this could mean that the new vaccine could be available for use within the next 5 to 10 years. Given the hype around any new vaccine however, one can’t help but also be cautious. History is replete with vaccines that showed potential in early phases but did not make it to market due to safety issues or inconsistent efficacy in later trials. But given the global health impact of rotavirus, these are risks worth taking. If this vaccine's promise is successful beyond initial trials, it could potentially save thousands of lives each year and significantly reduce the strain on healthcare systems globally. Amber Rudd: 'Don't call me a racist for talking about immigration' By Kim Thomas The Home Secretary has defended her government's plans to encourage companies to employ more British people, insisting they are not 'racist' and should not be 'politically incorrect' to discuss immigration. Speaking to The Sunday Times, Amber Rudd said questions about the kind of jobs and skills shortages British workers could fill are important and need addressing. She spoke out against the idea that the issue of immigration is 'off-limits', despite recent outcry over the government's new immigration policies. Her comments come as tensions rise over how best to address public concerns about the scale and impact of immigration. The government has been under pressure to balance the need for skilled workers, particularly in the health service and technology sectors, with demands to reduce overall net migration. Rudd was responding to recent backlash against proposed 'crackdowns' on immigration, particularly the idea that companies could be required to publish lists of foreign workers they employ. There has been criticism that the government's handling of the issue risks stigmatizing foreign workers and that similar measures in the past have been seen as divisive and potentially harmful to community relations. However, Rudd insisted that the focus was not about punishing businesses that employ foreign workers, but about addressing skills gaps and encouraging training for British workers. "We’re not talking about penalizing employers for employing foreign workers," she told the Sunday Times. "We’re saying let’s make sure we can train and hire more people from this country. The Advocate General, one of the European Union’s most senior legal advisors, made the ruling – which is not yet legally binding but is often followed by the European Court of Justice – in a case involving a media website in the Netherlands that had linked to a site hosting unauthorized Playboy photos. The case, brought to the courts by Playboy Enterprises, has been followed closely due to its potential impact on content sharing and linking practices online. The essential question at stake is whether a website can be liable for copyright infringement simply because it directs readers to content hosted elsewhere. The Advocate General’s opinion, which was issued recently, states that the mere act of providing a link to content that is already available online does not constitute an infringement. He argues that linking does not add a new "communication to the public," which is a key concept in EU copyright law. Essentially, if a work has already been made available to the public in one location, providing a link to it in another does not create a new public or cause a new infringement. However, this ruling comes with a caveat: it does not apply if the linking party is aware of the fact that the original content was made available without the copyright owner’s permission. In other words, if the linking site knew that the content was pirated or unauthorized, they could still be held liable for secondary infringement – particularly if they benefited financially from the link or actively encouraged users to access the pirated content. This ruling could be pivotal because if adopted by the European Court of Justice, it could set a precedent that provides some protection for websites that link to content without actively hosting it themselves. It could also clarify the inconsistent treatment of links across the EU, where some countries like Germany have been more restrictive and others like the UK have tended to be less so. The Netherlands, where the case originated, has also been seen as a particularly permissive jurisdiction in terms of linking. The Advocate General’s opinion seems to align with this trend, suggesting that linking should generally be permitted unless it can be shown to be directly contributing to an infringement. Critically, this ruling does not change the underlying principle that copyright holders have rights over their work. It does not permit websites to actively host or republish copyrighted material without permission. However, it provides a clearer distinction between passive linking (providing a simple link to already available content) and active publication or distribution of copyrighted material. The implications of this ruling could extend beyond Playboy and the media sector to any industry that creates and distributes content. Every weekend, across all the major sports, we witness moments of sheer brilliance that can boggle the mind. On the pitch, an athlete generates an absurd amount of speed and agility, evading tackle after tackle. On the tennis court, a player serves a ball with such precision and pace that it hardly leaves the opponent any time to react. On the golf course, a golfer drills a shot that finds the pin from an almost impossible distance. These moments of genius, that makes us pause and wonder, "how on earth did they do that?" Although such displays of exceptional skill and talent appear to be effortless and almost divine in its execution, the reality is far more grounded in hard work and relentless effort. Elite sport, even at the top, is not magic, despite how it may sometimes appear. Take, for example, Roger Federer, widely regarded as one of the greatest tennis players in history. His shots are a blend of power and precision that often seem almost otherworldly. Yet, watch him train, and you see a man who puts in hours of grueling work both on and off the court. He trains his mind as much as his body, honing his focus and strategy in ways that few others achieve or even attempt. In a similar vein, consider Usain Bolt, who seemed to break the laws of physics with his running speed. His sprinting prowess was assumed by many to be an innate talent. However, if you delve into his training regimen, it is clear that his speed results from a foundation of strength, power, and endurance built through rigorous training and an extraordinary work ethic. Even in team sports where the genius in play may be more distributed, the effort is no less relentless. Take the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo or Lionel Messi in soccer. Theirs doesn’t come from sporadic, sporadic bursts of brilliance; it’s the consistent application of their skill set, honed through years of practice and dedication. Whether it’s the way they control the ball, their tactical awareness, or their physical conditioning, each aspect of their game is a product of hours of training. Nonetheless, while effort and practice are undeniably crucial for reaching elite levels and performing at moments of greatness, there is also an X-factor — a unique innate ability that allows these athletes to do things others cannot. This is often what gets labeled as "talent." But what is less discussed, and what these athletes truly owe their careers to, is the relentless repetition of their craft, the grind that often goes unnoticed and unmentioned. Take, for example, the way a basketball player practices their free throws. The thousands of free throws thrown in silence, often alone, with no audience and no applause. It’s not glamourous, but it’s the foundation of their ability to hit clutch shots under pressure. The same applies to a golfer meticulously practicing their swing, making the necessary adjustments through thousands of repetitions. Or a football player running drills, over and over, to perfect the timing and precision of their passes. In this sense, the veneer of effortlessness that often surrounds elite sports performance is misleading. It is a cultivated illusion—a trusty result of the industrious, successful application of what is often mundane but essential work. Beyond the anecdotal examples of athletes, research supports this narrative. According to a model derived from extensive study, known as the 10,000-hour rule, it takes roughly 10,000 hours of "deliberate practice" to master a complex skill.

Rebekah Brooks: A study in vindication By: James Bennett Rebekah Brooks, former editor of the now-defunct News of the World, has spoken of her feelings of deep vindication following her complete acquittal of various charges related to phone hacking and other offences. A decade and a half of legal proceedings, media scrutiny, and questions about her conduct as one of Britain's most influential press figures has culminated in this momentous verdict. The Southwark Crown Court ruled that Brooks, along with her co-defendants, former News of the World executive director Cheryl Carter and News International chief security officer Mark Hanna, were not guilty of all charges. This included charges of conspiracy, misuse of private information, and perverting the course of justice. Brooks, who appeared visibly emotional as the verdict was read out, said she felt "relieved" and "vindicated". In a statement from her legal team, she expressed her gratitude toward the court and her supporters, while also acknowledging the impact this period has had on her life and those around her. "This has not been an easy road for me, my family, or my colleagues. But today feels like a validation of the facts. I am simply a journalist who wanted to do the best for my paper and my team. We worked hard, we followed the rules, and I am grateful to the court for seeing the evidence and clearing us of all charges," she said. The news sent ripples through the media landscape, with many seeing Brooks' vindication as a significant development in the ongoing story of the phone hacking scandal - a scandal that has reshaped the British press, led to significant media reforms, and saw the closure of one of the world's most widely circulated Sunday newspapers. Rebekah Brooks was at the helm of News of the World when it became clear that the publication had engaged in widespread phone hacking practices. These revelations, which exposed the private lives of celebrities, politicians, and even victims of violence and tragedies, led to public outrage and triggered the Leveson Inquiry into press practices and ethics, as well as a series of police investigations and trials. This trial dealt specifically with allegations that Cooke, Brooks, Carter, and Hanna conspired to remove and conceal evidence from police investigations into the phone hacking. Accused of hiding computers and other materials, these charges were seen by many as a more serious challenge for Brooks, given the potential for accusations of obstructing justice. Despite being cleared, Brooks acknowledged the controversy her role at the News of the World brought her. "I want to say to those who were affected by the practices at the News of the World during my time as editor, and the wider press industry as a whole, we did not get everything right. The rules of the game needed changing, and they have. I hope our industry continues to learn from this past and keeps improving," she stated. The reaction to her acquittal has been mixed. While some hail her as a figure successfully clearing her name, others remain critical, pointing to the wider implications of the phone hacking scandal and the necessity for press accountability. The British Newspaper Society welcomed the verdict as an important milestone, but stressed the need for continued vigilance and adherence to ethical standards in journalism. "This acquittal does not change the fact that indiscretions in our industry have led to significant consequences, including the Leveson Inquiry and subsequent reforms. We must continue to strive for transparent, responsible journalism," the society's statement read. Lawyers acting on behalf of phone-hacking victims, though disappointed by the verdict, said they would review the judgment in detail, considering potential appeals or further legal actions.

Britain implemented plain packaging in 2017, becoming one of the first countries to do so. Dr. Hannah Betts, a public health researcher at the University of Oxford and lead author of the review, stated that the removal of branding from cigarette packs "removes a major incentive for smoking, making it less attractive or appealing, particularly to young people." Betts continued, "The findings from this review suggest that plain packaging could be a cost-effective way to reduce smoking prevalence in the UK, particularly while the 'novelty' of the new packs remains at its highest." The review assessed the impact of plain packaging by analysing data from countries that have already implemented similar legislation, including Australia (2012), France (2016), and New Zealand (2018), as well as from experimental psychological studies. In the short term, the removal of cigarette brands could lead to quitting or reduced consumption due to a decreased perceived attractiveness of smoking; in the long term, plain packaging, coupled with other anti-smoking policies, could contribute to a declining prevalence of smoking among younger generations. As the second officer killed in cold blood in New York over the past month was laid to rest, hundreds of police officers made their feelings clear. They turned their backs on the city's mayor, Bill de Blasio, as he spoke at the funeral, a gesture that immediately sparked a firestorm of debate and controversy. The officers who defiantly turned their back on the mayor days after the funeral of fellow police officer Wenjian Liu were not just showing a simple act of disrespect but were making a public statement, of deep-seated fractiousness and mistrust between the police force and their leadership. The context is critical here. The shooting incident in which Liu and his partner Rafael Ramos were killed, has been seen by many in the police force as rooted in a narrative pushed by the mayor, that argues police brutality is systemic. It has been perceived by the officers as an unfair characterization and a blame on the entire police force for the actions of a few rogue officers. In the days immediately following the shooting, some police union leaders raised concerns that remarks made by the mayor and his administration were partly to blame for the tense situation, leading to an anti-police sentiment that they claim put their officers at greater risk. “It’s really quite simple,” a police union leader was quoted saying before the funeral. “The men and women who are showing their backs to the mayor are doing so because they feel betrayed by comments made by him and his administration. They don’t feel they’re being represented or supported, and that’s the core issue here.” The mayor, on the other hand, insists he supports the police and regrets the hurt caused by any statement made, but still calls for deep-seated societal issues regarding race and policing to be addressed. This is not the first time there have been incidents like this, where police officers have turned their backs on political figures in protest. However, the scale and visibility of this reaction to the mayor of the largest city in the USA, New York, is unprecedented. The decision of the officers to protest in such a visible manner during a solemn occasion like the funeral of a colleague is a sign of a relationship strained to the breaking point. It speaks to a deep-seated suspicion that the leadership, in this case the mayor’s office, is unwilling to stand by the men and women who put themselves on the line every day to keep the city safe. The implications of such a gesture go beyond a singular event or figure and raise broader questions about the structure of accountability, the influence of politics on public service, and the ongoing dialogue about race and policing in the United States. In the immediate aftermath, the response from the public and politicians has been mixed. Some have decried the officers’ actions as disrespectful, while others have seen it as a necessary form of protest. As the debate rages on, both sides will need to navigate the treacherous landscape of public relations, political influence, and genuine concern for the safety of both the public and the police officers who serve them. For the police, it's not just about a single comment or policy but about a sense of being sidelined, misunderstood, and at risk in a very dangerous job. For the mayor and his administration, it's about balancing the trust of the police with what they see as a necessary push for systemic reform in policing and society at large. The path forward will undoubtedly be complex and contentious. But what is clear is this: the gesture of turning backs at a funeral was not just about disrespect for a politician, but a desperate attempt to be heard in a society caught between the police, politicians, and the population they both serve

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), which is now into its 19th round, started in Pretoria yesterday. It will continue for over two weeks and will see hundreds of delegates from around the world discussing how best to preserve wildlife that is under threat from habitat destruction, climate change, and illegal trade. Yet, the issue of how to protect elephant populations has divided the community right down the middle. On one side, those pushing for measures to safeguard elephant populations. On the other, those advocating for controlled trade in elephant products, primarily ivory, claiming it could support conservation efforts. Kenya, and several other elephants range states, are pushing for all elephants in Africa to be classified as 'endangered' under CITES. They argue that the continued demand for ivory, despite legal domestic markets being closed in many countries, is driving poaching and threatening wild elephants. "The impact of the ivory trade on our elephant populations cannot be overstated," said Najib Balala, Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for Tourism and Wildlife. "Kenya lost over 100 elephants last year due to poaching alone, and if we continue to allow even the most basic forms of ivory trade, the consequences will be devastating." However, opposition to this approach comes from countries like Namibia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe. These nations argue that quotas for legal, controlled ivory trade can generate revenue for conservation efforts and provide an alternative to poaching. "We can only ensure the survival of elephants if they are worth something to the people who live alongside them," said Tamsin Fennell, leading the Namibian delegation. But it's not just about the elephant populations. For many communities, the elephant is a part of their economy and livelihood. In these countries, the controlled sale of ivory from natural mortality or culling could provide much-needed income to local communities. The legal ivory sales from stockpiles held by these countries were last permitted in 2016. Since then, some have built up significant stockpiles, valued at millions of dollars. The Zambian delegation argues that by monetizing these stocks – and reinvesting the profits into conservation efforts – local people might be less tempted to poach, as they would have a tangible stake in elephant protection. The global community, however, is not devoid of discord on this matter. Advocacy groups like the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) and the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) support a blanket ban on all international trade. "The concept of a 'controlled' ivory trade has proven to be a facade, just driving demand and poaching," said IFAW's Rob Lott. "Policymakers should focus on shutting down the trade entirely." But while the debate rages on, it's clear that the elephant – that magnificent, intelligent and iconic creature – is facing a crisis. According to a report presented at the conference, the African elephant population has declined by over 60% in the last three decades. If current trends continue, some fear that within our lifetimes, wild elephants could be a thing of the past. Lennon argues that equitable access to these products is a fundamental right and, more importantly, an absolute necessity for the inherent dignity of women. Lennon’s call to action comes at a time when period poverty has increasingly come into the spotlight. From the United States to Uganda, from Australia to the UK, activists and politicians are fighting to make menstrual products free or at least accessible for all. In the UK, the issue has gained significant attention over the last few years due to the tireless work of campaigners and the media. The path to this policy change isn't without its obstacles. Critics argue that providing free sanitary products would be an additional burden on the already strapped public purse. However, advocates insist that this thinking misses the point. They argue that when one considers the healthcare costs associated with infections and other issues caused by inadequate menstrual hygiene, providing free products becomes a cost-saving measure in the long run. Moreover, there are arguments that this move is necessary not just for health reasons, but for social equality. By providing free sanitary products, we are sending a strong message that the issues faced by menstruating women are important and worth addressing. It's about acknowledging that menstruation is a normal biological process, not something that should be shrouded in shame or cost. The policy proposed by MSP Lennon is a landmark step in recognizing this fact. Born in Cardiff in 1949, Rees' early years were marked by her love for the arts. Her father was involved in the Welsh theatre and her mother, a music teacher, instilled in her a passion for music and dance. This foundation influenced her decision to study at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London, where she honed her craft and began her illustrious acting career. Before Poldark, Rees had already carved out a successful stage and television career. She appeared in several British Television plays and series, including The Three Sports, The Cassandra Project, and Otley. However, it was her role as the fiery Demelza in Poldark that catapulted her to national fame. Poldark, based on Winston Graham's novels, was a hugely popular BBC drama that aired from 1975 to 1977. Rees’ portrayal of Demelza, the love interest of the titular character Ross Poldark, played by Robin Ellis, was both charming and feisty. The role showcased her talent and garnered her numerous accolades and awards, including the British Film Institute's Best Television Actress award in 1977. Furthermore, Rees also made a notable impact in the theatre. She appeared in several notable stage productions, including the world premiere of Harold Pinter's Betrayal at the National Theatre in 1978, and later, in 1988, she starred in the West End production of The Secret Rapture. Rees was not only a talented actress but also a gifted singer. She released an album of songs, 'Angharad Rees' in 1968, which included a range of popular songs of the era. Despite her success, Rees was also known for her humility and kindness. She was described by those who knew her as warm, down-to-earth, and generous with her time and talent. Her contribution to British television and theatre will not be forgotten. Rees was also vocal about her experience dealing with cancer. She was diagnosed with the disease for the second time after recovering from previously suffering and surviving breast cancer. She used her platform to raise awareness about cancer, its various forms, and the importance of early detection and treatment. In a statement released by her family, they mourned the loss of "a beautiful, deeply loved and generous soul who had given so much and who will be so deeply missed." They also expressed gratitude for the kindness shown to Rees during her illness and condolences to her friends and fans who knew and admired her work. While the passing of this beloved actress is mourned by many, her body of work continues to be remembered and cherished. Her performances in Poldark and beyond have provided countless hours of drama, humor, and romance to many across generations. As the tributes pour in, it is clear that Angharad Rees will be remembered not just as a talented actress but as a significant cultural figure of 1970s Britain. Her ability to bring complexity and warmth to a character as enduring as Demelza in Poldark is a testament to her skill and will undoubtedly continue to inspire acting students and fans alike. Fifteen firms from across Scotland have been "named and shamed" by the UK's Department for Work and Pensions for failing to pay staff at least the national minimum wage. These include several big businesses and small local enterprises, showing that no organisation is too big to be held to account. A particular disappointment, the DWP stated, was that many of these companies were already aware of the correct wage and yet still chose to break the law. The national minimum wage is a legal entitlement for most of the adult working population and is currently set at £6.19 for those aged 21 and over. This changes to a higher rate of £6.31 from 1st October 2013. The national living wage - the amount set independently to reflect the basic cost of living - is higher still and is to be introduced in 2016. As of now, however, the national minimum wage is the legal lower limit. For individual workers, being paid less than this amount can mean living below the poverty line, as the wage often does not cover the basic costs of living. For these Scottish workers, the consequences are very real. As Karen White, a worker in Glasgow who fell victim to wage underpayment recently stated, "It's a struggle to make ends meet when you're not being paid what you're owed." The fifteen companies involved have now been ordered to pay the arrears they owe their workers in total more than £140,000 - with the individual payments varying from hundreds to several thousand pounds. The DWP's statement also made clear that while many of these firms were repeat offenders, the sooner the money is paid, the less they will have to fork out in fines, which can reach as high as £5,000 per worker. The firms involved, it should be noted, come from a variety of sectors including food and drink, retail, and entertainment, and operate in different parts of Scotland, from Edinburgh and Glasgow to the Highlands and Islands. As one industry expert commented, "This action should serve as a stark warning to others. Employers who think they can ignore or bend the rules will be caught out and exposed." The UK's national minimum wage law has been changing the lives of thousands of workers since its introduction in 1998, though critics argue more needs to be done to ensure its enforcement. The Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, Iain Duncan Smith, pointed out that while zero prosecutions were recorded last year, 29 firms have been found and penalised so far in 2013. "Paying staff the minimum wage is not just the law, it's a moral obligation," he stated. "Where we find examples of workers being exploited, we will take action to correct it and make sure their rights are protected." As for the Scottish firms named, most have already begun to rectify their wage underpayment. Some however, like one Glasgow-based restaurant which owed over £5,000 to a single worker, have chosen not to comment on the situation. Others have expressed deep regret and acknowledged the importance of compliance with the law. The Egyptian authorities initially claimed that Regeni had died in a car accident, a story they quickly backed away from, suggesting instead that he had been killed in a fight over a taxi fare. However, this theory was dismissed due to evidence pointing to a more sinister scenario. The cause of his death, brutally tortured and with signs of prolonged beating, has been clarified as murder, but the circumstances surrounding Regeni's final days remain shrouded in mystery. Regeni had been researching the conditions of Egypt’s labour movement for Cambridge University and the American University in Cairo. His death has led his family and many others to believe that he was targeted because of his academic work. Egypt’s record on human rights has been a cause for concern over the past few years, ever since the Arab Spring protests in 2011 that ousted President Hosni Mubarak. Since the military coup of 2013, which led to the rise of current President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to power, Human Rights Watch and other international rights organizations have documented an alarming increase in arrests, detentions, and trials, often with little or no due process. The Italian government has strongly condemned the murder and has called for an "exhaustive inquiry" leading to full accountability for Regeni's death. The Italian Foreign Minister, Paolo Gentiloni, expressed deep concerns that Regeni's case may not be an isolated incident but rather the symptom of a broader climate of fear and repression in Egypt. The situation also serves as a stark reminder of the risks faced by journalists, human rights defenders, and researchers attempting to cover sensitive topics in Egypt today. The Regeni case is but the latest chapter in a changing story of repression in Egypt. As the country grapples with Islamic extremism, a struggling economy, and increasing influence from the global oil/power play, the government seems to be pushing for a more authoritarian rule, allegedly to maintain public order and stability. This strategy of censorship and repression, however, has manifested in high-profile cases like the arrest and conviction of journalists and activists, including several foreign nationals. Whether they are Egyptian or international, freedom of expression, assembly, and the right to a fair trial appear to be under constant threat. Every weekend, approximately 150 people are released from Welsh prisons - a routine spectacle that is rarely covered by today's headlines. However, what happens to these individuals after they exit the prison gates is of great concern. Figures from a various organizations, including charity organization 'Homeless Link', highlight the drastically high rates of homelessness among those who have served time. A recent report released by the charity states that there is a "chronic need" for more housing provision for individuals released from prison in Wales. The statistics are stark: a significant number of ex-prisoners are forced to sleep rough within days of release, due to a lack of support and adequate accommodation. This problem, while not exclusive to Wales, creates a cycle of reoffending - with many returning to prison due to the absence of stable housing. This is a trend that not only affects the individuals themselves but also their families, the broader community, and the taxpayer - as we invest in their initial incarceration and then repeatedly in reincarceration due to the failure to reintegrate them successfully. The charity also highlighted that while some Wales-based organizations provide support, these services are often limited in scale and scope. They proposed that major changes would be needed to accommodate the current volume of offenders released. Current figures suggest that around 14,300 people are currently sleeping rough across the UK as a whole, and a portion of this number is composed of ex-prisoners. Homeless Link’s research director, Pete Read, said, "This data tells a stark story. The current system is failing people – not just those in current need, but also their families and, ultimately, the wider community. Ex-prisoners, like all individuals, should have access to stable, affordable housing – not only to prevent homelessness but also to aid rehabilitation." One local organization in Wales, Ty Gobaith, the largest probation service provider in the country, has been working hard to provide accommodation and support for prison leavers. However, they echo the views of Homeless Link: that there is still a gap. Sarah Williams, a representative from Ty Gobaith, said: "We see first-hand the struggles that our clients face. We try to offer support as best we can, but accommodation is always a challenge. With more housing provision and targeted support, we believe we can make a real difference." The current support for prison leavers is not uniformly adequate across the UK, with each region working independently. In Wales, local authorities, public health bodies, and third-sector organizations are all overwhelmed by the demand, and resources are stretched. The charity’s report suggests that this situation is not just an issue of funding, but also one of complete and holistic support. Head of policy at the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA), Helen Wilkinson, stated, “The issue of housing ex-offenders is a key concern for local authorities. While we are doing our best with limited resources, the demand far exceeds capacity. Title: The Evolutionary Artisans: Uncovering the Forgotten Culture of Primate Archaeology The study of human history is often filled with tales of ancient civilizations, grand monuments, and sophisticated artefacts that showcase the ingenuity and creativity of our species. However, a relatively new field of research now seeks to challenge this anthropocentric view of history: primate archaeology. Primates, and more specifically non-human primates such as chimpanzees, bonobos, and capuchin monkeys, have demonstrated behaviour that, until recently, we had only ascribed to humans. The pursuits of these creatures are not limited to mere survival - they are complex, multifaceted, and, yes, 'cultural' in nature. For instance, chimpanzees are known to create tools in order to hunt, to use stone to crack nuts, among other activities. These actions indicate a capacity for innovation, problem-solving, and even the preservation of learned knowledge across generations - all components of what we might term 'culture'. Bonobos, on the other hand, have been observed engaging in complex communication, conflict resolution processes similar to human ones, and even cooperative hunting. These actions far exceed what was previously expected from these or any other non-human primates. But this is where the unusual-sounding field of primate archaeology comes into play. It's also worth noting the cultural aspects of Corbyn's leadership. He was often seen as out of step with the wider public's views. Sixty years ago, the world marveled at a cinematic masterpiece that was both a brazen satire of Cold War politics and an uproarious comedy. "Dr Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb," directed by the indispensable Stanley Kubrick, now stands as one of the greatest film comedies ever made. It’s hard to believe that it was originally released in 1964, but the poignancy and relevance of Kubrick’s work only appears to grow stronger with time. The film, based on Peter George’s novel "Red Alert," is a farcical representation of the societal and political anxieties that gripped the world during the Cold War. It offers a scathing critique of the destructive potential of nuclear warfare, questioning the rationality of armaments policy through a lens of absurdist comedy. The film tells the story of a delusional US Air Force General Jack D. Ripper (played by Sterling Hayden), who orders a nuclear strike on the Soviet Union. His paranoia about a communist conspiracy to fluoridate US water supplies leads him to reactivate Plan R, an automatic protocol for launching a nuclear attack. As events spiral out of control, those left to prevent or respond to the impending catastrophe struggle with the absurdity of it all and the dire consequences of their actions. Kubrick’s genius lies in his ability to balance heavy subjects with absurdity. The script, co-written by Kubrick, Terry Southern, and Peter George, is peppered with dark humor and dialogue that still elicits chuckles today. The scenes in the War Room, particularly those between the likes of President Merkin Muffley (a brilliant Peter Sellers), General Turgidson (a savage George C. Scott), and the eponymous Dr Strangelove himself, are filled with wit, subtext, and satire that remain timeless. The influence of "Dr Strangelove" on popular culture cannot be overstated. It has influenced countless filmmakers, from satire specialists like Monty Python to auteurs like Quentin Tarantino, and even modern-day TV shows like "Veep" and "The Good Place." The character of Dr Strangelove, played by Sellers in multiple roles, including a wheelchair-bound, Nazi sympathizing former scientist, is an iconic symbol of the film. Kubrick’s commitment to realism also sets the film apart. For example, he paid considerable attention to the design and aesthetics of the B-52 bomber interiors, using the actual plans sent to him by the U.S. Air Force. The meticulous detail and almost documentary-level realism of the aircraft and the military facilities serve to heighten the satire. If the futility and horror of nuclear war weren’t already apparent, the film makes sure they are, all under the guise of black comedy. The film’s themes are still pertinent today. The Cold War has ended, but the threat of nuclear conflict remains, however unlikely. Moreover, the film also explores themes of authoritarianism, paranoia, and the potential for disaster when militaristic thinking trumps diplomacy. General Ripper’s paranoia about a communist conspiracy, for example, echoes current global fears and debates about misinformation and disinformation campaigns. "Dr Strangelove" is successful because it refuses to take itself too seriously. It’s a comedy, but its humor isn’t just for the sake of humor; it’s a tool to dissect the irrationalities of war and the madness of the nuclear arms race. The film acknowledges the ludicrous nature of its subject matter and lingers on the tension, the absurdity, and the undercurrent

"This is not just any ordinary piece of legislation," barrister Lord Pannick QC, representing the lead claimant Gina Miller, told the court. "This is about the competence of parliament to authorise the government to take a step that will inevitably lead to a fundamental change in our constitutional arrangement and the rights of citizens." The hearing brought together a diverse group of individuals including a claimant who argued that her rights as a citizen - including the right to vote in EU elections - would be affected by this process. A university professor raised concerns about the academic freedoms that could be compromised in a post-Brexit world, while a British expatriate in the EU questioned the implications on her right to live and work abroad. The government's position, presented by attorney general Jeremy Wright, was that the issue was not about the merits of Brexit, but about who had the authority to trigger the process. He argued that the executive has the power to make and withdraw from international treaties, including the EU treaties, without needing parliamentary approval. However, this does not cover legislation, but invoking Article 50 is more of a formal declaration of intent rather than legislation changing the law. The court's judges, including Lord Chief Justice Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd, were asked to consider not just the immediate issue of parliamentary approval but also the broader constitutional implications of allowing executive action without parliamentary nod. Lawyers also explored the concept of 'prerogative powers', those traditionally held by the monarch but now mostly used by the government. These powers are not set out in law, but based on tradition and precedent. The claimants argued that while these powers still exist, they have been considerably diminished in scope over the years, especially as parliament gained more power. They stressed that for such a significant constitutional move like Brexit, parliamentary approval should be a requirement. The hearing also touched on the role of the referendum, with the government arguing that it represented the will of the people and thus provided a mandate for the government to act. However, the claimants pointed out that the referendum itself did not legally bind the government to trigger Article 50 and that the UK's constitutional structure requires parliamentary approval for such actions. "The referendum was advisory, and while it sets the mood of the country, it does not replace the rule of law or the need for parliamentary scrutiny," Lord Pannick said. Philipp Hammond, the UK's Foreign Secretary, has declared that achieving necessary reforms to the European Union via treaty changes is essential; these amendments are what he perceives will be required to meet the "German requirements." This statement, made during various high-profile media appearances, including the BBC's "Today" programme and Sky News' "Sophy Ridge" programme, questions the status of EU treaty amendments in the context of the country's future relations with the bloc. "What the Germans are indicating they need to see is some of the things that the British side are seeking to deal with in terms of their concerns about the functioning of the EU," Hammond elaborated. "I think it will be necessary to make some change, to make a treaty change in order to deliver on some of the requirements that the Germans are setting out." The implications of Hammond's assertion have been the subject of much debate among political commentators and EU observers in the wake of the recent UK-EU negotiations. Critics argue that such requirements could be overly coercive and serve to undermine the UK's sovereignty intentions, which were a central pillar of the Leave campaign. However, supporters of the government's negotiation stance see such treaty changes as a means to achieve concessions that might justify the costs and complexities associated with leaving the EU. Hammond's statement comes amid ongoing EU-UK negotiations on the terms of Britain's exit from the union. As both sides attempt to find common ground on sensitive subjects such as the rights of EU citizens in the UK post-Brexit and the financial settlement, the prospect of treaty changes adds an additional layer of complexity to the negotiating process. The British side has prioritised the need for regulatory divergence to allow for, among other things, more autonomy in areas such as agriculture and fisheries. Hammond's comments suggest that the UK government may have identified treaty changes as a key lever to gain the necessary flexibility in these areas. However, it is not without its challenges. The EU, particularly the European Commission, has traditionally been resistant to treaty changes due to the perceived complexity and the potential for opening up broader discussions about the future of the union. The process, as outlined in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), involves a Council decision followed by ratification by all member states according to their constitutional requirements—a process that can be lengthy and unpredictable. For instance, failed attempts to ratify the Treaty of Lisbon in 2007 were illustrative of the potential roadblocks. In this light, Hammond's assertion can be interpreted as a tactical move to set the expectations for what the UK believes are the minimum prerequisites for a successful Brexit, and potentially to gauge the EU's flexibility on such changes. Yet, the feasibility and the real-world practicality of such changes remains questionable. Moreover, there are also internal political considerations in the UK. Hammond's comments can be seen as a move to rally support across different factions within the Conservative party and broader political spectrum that have often demanded more autonomy or sovereignty from the EU. By positioning any potential treaty changes as part of a negotiated outcome, the government can potentially argue that they are securing the best possible terms for the UK, potentially mitigating criticism from those who believe a harder Brexit—essentially a no deal—would be preferable. However, the difficulty lies in balancing these internal UK political requirements with what will be successful in negotiations with the EU, 27 member states each with their own priorities and limitations. Hammond acknowledged this challenge, but his statement indicates a high level of commitment from the UK side to engage in what would likely be a contentious and time-consuming process. Critics have also pointed out that by advocating for treaty changes, the UK may be walking into a trap.

In India, the sedition law, rooted deeply in the country's colonial past, continues to be wielded today in ways that are both bewildering and concerning. The Indian Penal Code, which includes Section 124A on sedition, was first formulated in 1860 during British rule and aimed to suppress dissent against British rule. In today's India, this law seems to serve a different purpose, and the reasons for its invocation are increasingly diverse and sometimes seemingly arbitrary. Recent examples of its application are fractious. A citizen in Tamil Nadu was charged for “liking” a Facebook post that allegedly criticized a yoga guru. This scenario raises fundamental questions about the limits of free speech on the internet. The act of engaging with an online post, often considered a casual or even involuntary action under today’s social media norms, is now seen as sufficient for triggering legal action. Similarly, following a cricket match where India’s arch-rival, Pakistan, won, some fans were arrested for cheering the rival team. This has sparked debates over whether the law should extend to sports and whether cheering for a competing team should constitute sedition. The logic behind such arrests seems to rest on the assumption that such actions could potentially cause or incite disaffection against the state. Furthermore, there have been instances where drawing cartoons or asking provocative questions in university exams have been acted against under the sedition law. The cartoons in particular have garnered international attention; the medium itself is often used for satire, criticism, and often, the cartoons in question neither explicitly called for violence nor did they incite hate towards any community or religious group, challenging the crux of sedition in itself: the instigation of violence or rebellion against the state. In a move that blurred the lines between patriotism and the law, a man was also arrested for not standing up during the national anthem in a cinema. The incident reignites the debate over what constitutes appropriate behaviour and if one’s perceived lack of respect towards national symbols should be legal measured, let alone punished under a law designed to stop armed revolt against the state. The amplification of these incidents reflects a worrying trend where the sedition law is being used to confront a wide and often arbitrary range of actions. Critics of the law argue that such broad applications disproportionately target individuals who may be exercising their rights to free speech, expression, or even just their inalienable right to choose what they do in their personal time. Historically, the law has been used against political dissidents, activists, and journalists. However, as India increasingly grapples with a pluralistic society and the complexities of cultural, political, and social debates in the digital age, these recent events highlight a concerning escalation of the law's use against seemingly innocuous acts. Legal experts and human rights advocates argue that the sedition law in its present form has the potential to stifle dissent and curtail free speech. They point out that the application of the law must be carefully balanced against the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution of India, including the right to freedom of speech and expression. They argue that punishing actions that do not directly incite violence or pose a clear and present danger to the state undermines these constitutional guarantees. Currently, local authorities are forced to ration available funding, meaning that only individuals deemed to have the most severe or critical needs receive support. This situation has led to a plethora of negative outcomes, from delayed discharges from hospitals due to insufficient care provided for when patients are ready to return home, to rising rates of missed appointments and potential health deteriorations for those left without the necessary support in their own homes. The monarchy, which had ruled the Persian nation for well over two millenniums, was overthrown in a revolution that swept the country. The revolution was not just a political upheaval, but a profound cultural and social transformation. This revolution, led by the Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, would lead to the establishment of the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Iranian monarchy, set up in 1925 by Reza Shah Pahlavi, had become increasingly autocratic and dependent on Western, particularly American, support. It was a period marked by rapid modernization attempts, often at the cost of traditional values and religious beliefs. This led to resentment among a wide section of the population, particularly amongst the clergy, but also amongst intellectuals, students, and the working class. They saw the monarchy as distant and out of touch with the needs and values of the people. The Islamic Republic, established by the Ayatollah Khomeini, was premised on the principle of “velayat-e faqih” or “guardianship of the jurist,” which firmly placed political power in the hands of religious leaders, particularly the Supreme Leader. Ayatollah Khomeini's return from exile in February 1979 became the catalyst for the fall of the monarchy. Millions took to the streets in support, and within days, the regime collapsed. However, the transition from monarchy to Islamic republic was not as smooth as it initially seemed. There were significant power struggles among different factions of the revolutionaries, each with their own understanding of the new order. The Islamic Republic that emerged was a complex hybrid of religious and democratic elements, with a constitution that provided for a president and parliament, but also placed significant influence and powers in the hands of religious leaders, notably the Supreme Leader. The first Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Khomeini, played a crucial role in shaping the early years of the Islamic Republic. His charisma, leadership skills, and unique blend of religious and political authority held the country together in its most tumultuous moments. While the first years of the Islamic Republic were marked by economic and political challenges, including a devastating eight-year war with Iraq, the regime persevered, often in part due to the strong and broadly felt grievances against the former monarchy and the perceived support it received internationally. The Ayatollah's death in 1989 led to the appointment of Ali Khamenei as the new Supreme Leader. Khamenei has since played a more subtle and behind-the-scenes role, often acting as a unifying figure and arbiter among competing factions. However, the concentration of power in the hands of the Supreme Leader and the clergy has also been a point of contention both within Iran and internationally. There have been periods of repression, including against political dissidents, women's rights activists, and religious minorities. The government has often justified these actions as necessary to preserve the Islamic character and stability of the state. This access comes with certain responsibilities and rules - for instance, about environmental standards, workers' rights, and regulations governing everything from food safety to financial services. Leave campaigners often argue that these regulations are overly burdensome and stifle business, while supporters of remaining in the EU stress the benefits that these rules provide, such as a level playing field for businesses across the bloc and higher consumer safety standards. One major concern is the potential impact on trade. If the UK were to leave the EU, it would have to renegotiate its relationship with the EU - and potentially many or even all of the other countries with which the EU has a trade agreement. This could be a complex and time-consuming process. Some economists worry that the UK might struggle to secure as favorable terms in any new trade deals, in part because the UK alone is a much smaller market than the EU as a whole. However, some Leave campaigners argue that without the constraints of EU law, the UK could negotiate its own, more favorable trade agreements with other countries in the rest of the world more quickly and independently. Another key area of focus is the question of tariffs and trade barriers. If the UK doesn't secure a deal that allows free trade with the EU, we could potentially face higher tariffs or non-tariff barriers, which would make UK goods more expensive for EU consumers. Conversely, EU businesses seeking to trade with the UK might also face additional barriers and increased costs, which could also have a negative impact on EU consumers. On the other hand, some Leave campaigners argue that the benefits of independence would outweigh any potential negative economic impacts. For instance, some suggest that the UK could save money previously spent on EU membership, although this money would still be required to run the country, invest in public services, and maintain social safety nets. Others say that being outside the EU could give the UK more flexibility in areas like trade, regulation, and the use of subsidy rules designed to support particular industries, particularly agriculture and fishing. The unfolding crisis deepens as first responders grapple with the emotional repercussions of one of the UK's worst fires in modern history, the Victoria Derbyshire programme has learned. The scope of the situation is stark: the London Fire Brigade has never before had to deploy this many counselors to support its personnel. The normal practice is to provide immediate support via the organisation's internal trauma service, but this secondary reinforcement suggests a level of trauma severity that goes far beyond routine incident aftermath support. The counselors have been brought in to work alongside the brigade's existing trauma support team, which normally deals with the day-to-day emotional fallout from firefighting. This includes dealing with the deaths and injuries seen in line of duty, but the scale of the horror following the Grenfell Tower fire has necessitated an unprecedented response. For context, the fire razed the 24-story tower block in Kensington, West London, on 14 June, 2017, resulting in the deaths of at least 71 residents. The images and accounts that emerged from the disaster site have haunted the public conscience, with numerous calls for justice, investigations and changes to building and fire safety practices. As news of this high-level support becomes public, it underscores the gravity of the job's emotional toll. Firefighters are often seen as masculine, stoic figures - but the reality is different. After incidents like Grenfell, where the rescue attempts were hampered by the scale of the fire and the speed at which it spread, first responders can be left with feelings of guilt, survivor's guilt, anger and a deep empathy for the victims. While the number of firefighters directly involved in the rescue and recovery efforts from Grenfell has not been publicly disclosed, it is understood to be in the hundreds. Each one may be dealing with the emotional impact in different ways. More broadly, those supporting firefighters and the wider public are also susceptible to what is known as secondary stress. Nonetheless, this additional counseling support is a testament to the brigade's recognition of the importance of mental health support for first responders - a stance that has likely been influenced by the aftermath of other major incidents such as 9/11 and the investigations that followed into the impact of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) on first responders. The public remains keenly aware of the ongoing demand for answers and the need for change and strengthening of fire safety regulations. The investigation into Grenfell, led by the Grenfell Tower Inquiry, has already taken 287 days and is expected to continue for several years. This ongoing process is likely contributing to the stress felt by the firefighters who went into action to save lives on that fateful night. To this end, the support for firefighters goes beyond the immediate practical need for trauma counseling. It signals a broader shift in understanding and addressing the mental health impacts of emergency work. Title: Gareth Gwenlan, Legendary Producer of 'Only Fools and Horses', Passes Away at 79 The British television industry has lost one of its stalwarts after the news broke of Gareth Gwenlan's passing. Known for his indelible work on one of Britain's most beloved and iconic sitcoms, 'Only Fools and Horses', Gwenlan was 79 at the time of his death. A veteran of the industry, his career spanned several decades and saw him work on a slew of popular British television series. Yet, it is 'Only Fools and Horses', which keeps coming up in conversations when people speak of his immense contribution to television. Gareth Gwenlan was born in 1943 in St Helens, Merseyside. His journey into television wasn't immediate; he initially worked in the steel industry, as was common amongst young men in places like St Helens during the post-war era. However, his passion for storytelling and television led him to move to London in the 70s where he decided to pursue a career in television production. After a brief stint at Granada TV, Gwenlan joined the production team of 'Only Fools and Horses' in 1985. Initially, he was an associate producer before taking over the reins as the programme's producer from 1986 until its end in 2003. 'Only Fools and Horses' documented the escapades of brothers Del Boy and Rodney Trotter as they navigated life, business, and the streets of Peckham through a combination of wit, charm, and the occasional (but often unintended) moral lesson. Gwenlan's contribution to the series' success is substantial. He was instrumental in shaping the characters, contexts, and narrative arcs that defined the show's enduring appeal. His ability to balance heartwarming humor with social commentary ensured 'Only Fools and Horses' didn't just entertain but also offered insightful commentary on British life during the 80s and 90s. The series racked up numerous awards and accolades during his tenure as producer, including several BAFTAs. It became a cultural phenomenon, beloved by audiences of all ages, thanks in no small part to Gwenlan's ability to maintain the show's tone and quality through its 22-years-long run. His death has brought forward tributes from industry colleagues, former cast members, and fans alike, each expressing their gratitude for the years of laughter 'Only Fools and Horses' has brought into their lives. John Challis, who played the character of Boycie in the show, expressed his grief over the loss of a friend and colleague. "Gareth was a true professional and a kind and generous man who had a sense of humor to match," Challis said. "I feel privileged to have worked alongside him and for him on that remarkable series." Actress Pauline Fowles, who played the role of Carol, Del's love interest, remembered Gwenlan fondly. "Gareth was the glue that held 'Only Fools and Horses' together for so long. He had a keen sense of humor and a youthful spirit that made him very much at ease with the cast and crew at any age." The passing of Gareth Gwenlan marks the end of an era in British television production. His work will undoubtedly continue to bring joy to viewers for generations to come. The proposed law, dubbed the 'Tax Certainty Act', is set to be a central part of the Conservative's election manifesto should they return to power. It's designed as a pledge to resist any pressures to raise the main three taxes over the course of the next parliamentary term. But not everyone agrees. Critics argue that such a law could handcuff future governments in responding effectively to changing economic conditions.
